title: When the misls quarreled
hook: as danger faded, rivalry grew between the misls

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ramgarhia towers, part of a bunga, plain brick lookouts built to guard the Harmandir. Your line was guarding towers. What precious thing did you stand guard over? Today, the story turns a little sour. Day nine hundred three.

A family pulls together beautifully at a funeral or in a hospital waiting room. Everyone brings food, nobody keeps score. Then the crisis passes, and months later two siblings aren't speaking over who got the good china. Sikh histories tell a story with the same shape. For a long time the misls were hunted, and they rode together because they had to. Then the hunters grew weaker, the misls held land, and the old enemy was no longer at the gate. Today: when the misls quarreled.
screen: `TOGETHER IN THE CRISIS.` → `APART WHEN IT PASSES.` → `THE MISLS HOLD THE LAND.`

segments.voice: Here's how Sikh histories describe the turn. While the danger was great, the bands needed one another. They met as the Sarbat Khalsa, agreed a gurmata, and rode under shared leaders. But once the misls held territory, each chief had something to lose, and something to gain at a neighbor's expense. Border villages. River crossings. Revenue. Marriages that tied one house to another, or failed to. The quarrels were not about faith. The chiefs bowed at the same Harmandir and heard the same scripture. They were about land and pride and who would lead. One story shows it. Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, the builder of yesterday's towers, was, Sikh histories say, pushed out of his lands for a time by rival chiefs, men who had once ridden beside him, and he lived beyond the Sutlej until he could come back. Other misls fought and made peace and fought again. The gatherings at Amritsar grew harder to hold together. Now set that beside the scripture they shared. In a hymn of Guru Arjan in the Guru Granth Sahib, on Ang 1299, the singer says, in paraphrase, that no one is his enemy and no one a stranger; he has come to get along with everyone. The chiefs heard the same scripture at the same Harmandir. Hearing it didn't stop the quarrels. That's the honest part of this story, and it's the part worth keeping. Unity under pressure is real. But it's easier than unity at ease. When the shared danger lifts, the old grudges find room. Danger gone, rivalry grew.
screen: `THE DANGER LIFTED.` · `LAND, PRIDE AND WHO WOULD LEAD.` · `RAMGARHIA PUSHED ACROSS THE SUTLEJ.` · `NO ONE IS MY ENEMY.` · then, large: `DANGER GONE, RIVALRY GREW.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with one rivalry. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you've drifted into competing with, or quietly resenting: a sibling, a coworker, an old friend, another parent at the school gate. Remember a time you were on the same side. Then ask what the rivalry is really about. It may be small. Land, pride, who leads. Choose one small move that would cool it: a compliment, a message, letting them win one. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

Sarbat Khalsa, the gathering that once bound the misls. Once danger faded, they quarreled over land and leadership, even sharing one scripture. This week: the Karorsinghia, the Shaheedan, the Phulkian states, twice a year at Amritsar, the bungas, the Ramgarhia towers, and the quarrels. Today's word.
Your line: danger gone, rivalry grew. Today, heal one rivalry, even a little. Send the message, give the compliment, or let them have this one. Day nine hundred three.

howItsDone: Sikh histories tell the misl rivalries frankly, and Sikhs read Guru Arjan's hymn on Ang 1299 of the Guru Granth Sahib about having no enemy and no stranger.

the bands start fighting each other over land and pride.

fork.reveal: as danger faded, rivalry grew. the chiefs who had ridden together fought over territory, though they shared the same scripture.
